items.title: Morning Brief: FOMC begins as Boeing and S&P Global report
items.dek: The Fed's two-day meeting starts today, with the decision due Wednesday; Boeing and S&P Global reported third-quarter results.
key_points: Federal Reserve calendar: FOMC meeting begins today and concludes Oct. 28 at 2:00 p.m. ET, with a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET; no Fed speeches are listed for Oct. 27-31.
Today's Fed releases: H.6 money stock and commercial paper at 1:00 p.m. ET, and H.15 interest rates at 4:15 p.m. ET.
H.15 on Oct. 23: 10-year Treasury yield 5.00%, 2-year 4.69%, effective federal funds rate 3.88%.
Boeing Q3: revenue $24,188M versus $23,270M; GAAP diluted loss per share $(0.26) versus $(7.14); free cash flow $464M; record backlog of $745B.
S&P Global Q3: revenue $3,678M versus $3,443M; adjusted diluted EPS $4.58 versus $4.20; 2026 adjusted EPS guidance raised to $17.70-$17.95.
talking_points: The Federal Reserve starts a two-day meeting today and announces its decision Wednesday at 2:00 p.m. Eastern, so everyday investors should expect rate headlines and a press conference at 2:30 p.m. that day.

Boeing reported a smaller quarterly loss per share than a year ago and generated $464 million of free cash flow, showing that cash generation and reported profit can move differently in the same quarter.

S&P Global raised its 2026 adjusted earnings guidance while lowering its GAAP range, a reminder that companies report several earnings measures and investors should check which one a headline is using.
body: The Federal Reserve's October calendar puts the Federal Open Market Committee at the center of the week. The two-day meeting begins today, and the calendar lists its conclusion on Oct. 28 at 2:00 p.m. ET, followed by a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET. The same calendar lists no speeches or discussions between Oct. 27 and Oct. 31, so the Wednesday decision and press conference are the scheduled public communications of the week.

body.h: Fed releases and the rate backdrop

body: Today's Fed data schedule includes H.6 money stock and commercial paper at 1:00 p.m. ET and the daily H.15 interest-rate release at 4:15 p.m. ET. The most recent H.15 figures, for Oct. 23, show the effective federal funds rate at 3.88%, unchanged from Oct. 22. The 2-year Treasury constant maturity yield was 4.69%, up from 4.65%, and the 10-year was 5.00%, up from 4.96%. By our calculation the 2-year yield sat 0.81 percentage point above the effective fed funds rate, and the 10-year sat 0.31 percentage point above the 2-year. Later this week the H.4.1 balance sheet report arrives Thursday at 4:30 p.m. ET and the H.8 report on commercial bank assets and liabilities follows Friday at 4:15 p.m. ET.

Boeing's third-quarter release reported revenue of $24,188 million, compared with $23,270 million a year earlier, an increase of 3.9% by our calculation. GAAP diluted loss per share was $(0.26), versus $(7.14) in the third quarter of 2025, and core loss per share, a non-GAAP measure, was $(0.34) versus $(7.47). Operating cash flow was $1,496 million versus $1,123 million, and non-GAAP free cash flow was $464 million versus $238 million. Boeing said total company backlog grew to a record $745 billion, including over 6,300 commercial airplanes.

S&P Global reported third-quarter revenue from continuing operations of $3,678 million versus $3,443 million, up 6.8% by our calculation. GAAP diluted EPS from continuing operations was $4.45 versus $3.54, and adjusted diluted EPS was $4.58 versus $4.20. The company raised its 2026 guidance for total revenue growth to 7.4% to 8.4% and for adjusted diluted EPS to $17.70 to $17.95, while its GAAP diluted EPS range moved down to $16.25 to $16.50 from $16.35 to $16.60.

RadNet announced an agreement to acquire ONRAD, a teleradiology and in-hospital radiology staffing provider, for $350 million in cash and 5 million RadNet shares, plus an earnout of up to $210 million tied to 2027 EBITDA. The company expects the transaction to close in early 2027, subject to customary regulatory review and closing conditions.
Taken together, the day's scheduled items are sparse on official economic data and heavy on corporate reporting, with the Fed's Wednesday decision the main event on the official calendar.

items.title: Morning Brief: EQT-Range tops a deal-heavy Monday as FOMC week begins
items.dek: The Fed's calendar is quiet until Wednesday's decision, while EQT, Ovintiv and Corxel announced deals and HBT Financial reported.
key_points: Federal Reserve calendar: FOMC meets Oct. 27-28; decision Oct. 28 at 2:00 p.m. ET, press conference at 2:30 p.m.; no speeches listed Oct. 23-31.
Today's Fed releases: commercial paper at 1:00 p.m. ET; H.10 foreign exchange rates and H.15 interest rates at 4:15 p.m.; H.6 money stock follows tomorrow at 1:00 p.m.
EQT to acquire Range Resources: 0.987 EQT shares per Range share; pro forma enterprise value over $50B; $325M base annual synergies within two years; close expected Q1 2027.

Ovintiv to acquire Logan Energy for C$1.40 per share in cash, about C$1.26B (US$890M) including expected net debt; Corxel US and Amanat Acquisition Corp announced a business combination with about $377M expected gross proceeds.
Earnings: HBT Financial Q3 net income $31.4M, or $0.86 per diluted share, versus $19.8M and $0.63; Amkor reports after the close, call at 5:00 p.m. ET.
talking_points: The Federal Reserve meets October 27 and 28, with its policy decision scheduled for 2:00 p.m. ET on the 28th, followed by a press conference at 2:30 p.m., so that is the date to watch.
EQT's deal for Range Resources is all stock, meaning Range holders receive EQT shares instead of cash, and the companies expect the combination to close in the first quarter of 2027 after approvals.
HBT Financial's net interest margin rose to 4.35% from 4.13% a year ago, showing how a bank's earnings depend on the gap between what it earns on loans and pays on deposits.
body: Monday opens with a light official calendar and a busy corporate one. The Federal Reserve Board's October calendar shows two statistical releases today: commercial paper at 1:00 p.m. ET and the H.10 foreign exchange rates at 4:15 p.m., alongside the daily H.15 interest-rate release at 4:15 p.m. The same calendar lists no speeches between October 23 and 31.

The Federal Open Market Committee meets October 27 and 28. The calendar lists the policy decision at 2:00 p.m. ET on October 28 and the press conference at 2:30 p.m. Before that, the H.6 money stock release is due at 1:00 p.m. ET tomorrow, and the weekly H.4.1 balance sheet report follows on Thursday at 4:30 p.m. Bank balance sheet data from the H.8 comes out Friday at 4:15 p.m.

Natural gas produced the largest announcement. EQT said each Range Resources share will be exchanged for 0.987 EQT shares, leaving EQT holders with about 73% of the combined company and Range holders about 27%. EQT put the pro forma enterprise value at over $50 billion, expects $325 million of base annual synergies within two years, and expects the transaction to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory and shareholder approvals. The release gives no dollar purchase price, so the $50 billion describes combined size rather than the value of the deal.

Separately, Ovintiv agreed to acquire Logan Energy for C$1.40 per share in cash, a total value of about C$1.26 billion, or about US$890 million, including Logan's expected net debt at closing. Ovintiv described about 266,000 net acres in the Montney oil window and Logan production of about 20 MBOE/d. Logan will spin out Logan Oil Corp. to its shareholders, and closing is expected early in the first quarter of 2027.

In biotech, Corxel US and Amanat Acquisition Corp, a special purpose acquisition company, announced a definitive business combination. The release cites about $75 million in Amanat's trust account and an expected PIPE of about $300 million, for roughly $377 million of gross proceeds if no Amanat shareholders redeem. No pro forma valuation was disclosed, and closing is expected in the first half of 2027.

HBT Financial reported third-quarter net income of $31.4 million, or $0.86 per diluted share, versus $19.8 million, or $0.63, a year earlier. Its net interest margin was 4.35% versus 4.13%, and it said Tri-County Financial Group's stockholders vote on HBT's pending acquisition of Tri-County on October 29. After the close, Amkor Technology is scheduled to release third-quarter results, with its conference call at 5:00 p.m. ET.

One gap in this morning's brief: the Treasury's auction schedule and the latest FRED rate series could not be read in this run, so rate levels and auction details are left out rather than carried over from earlier days.

items.title: The Close: Autos trim outlooks, Atlanta's FHLB grows its balance sheet
items.dek: Autoliv and Gentex reported softer profits on flat sales, while FHLB Atlanta and Orchid Island posted opposite results from mortgage-linked balance sheets.
key_points: Autoliv: Q3 net sales $2,693M vs. $2,706M; diluted EPS $2.13 vs. $2.28; 2026 adjusted operating margin guided to around 10.5%.
Gentex: Q3 sales $647.7M vs. $655.2M; 2026 revenue now about $2.65B vs. $2.65B-$2.75B before.
FHLB Atlanta: Q3 net income $126M vs. $155M; total assets $166.7B vs. $146.2B at Dec. 31, 2025.
Orchid Island: Q3 net loss of $178.9M, or $(0.90) per share, vs. net income of $72.1M a year earlier.
talking_points: Autoliv and Gentex both reported roughly flat sales but lower profit per share, which shows that costs and mix can matter as much as revenue when you read a company's quarterly results.
Gentex lowered its 2026 gross margin range to 34.0% to 34.5% and cited higher precious metal costs, a reminder that raw material prices can change a company's outlook even when demand is steady.
Orchid Island swung to a quarterly loss while its book value fell to $6.02 per share, so investors in mortgage-linked funds should look at book value and dividends together, not income alone.
body: Friday's company reports pointed to a familiar pattern: sales that held roughly steady while profit measures slipped, plus two very different results from mortgage-linked balance sheets.

Autoliv reported third-quarter net sales of $2,693 million versus $2,706 million a year earlier, a decline of 0.5% by our calculation. Operating income was $254 million versus $267 million, down 4.9%, and diluted EPS was $2.13 versus $2.28. Adjusted diluted EPS was $2.19 versus $2.32. For 2026 the company guides organic sales growth of around 0%, an adjusted operating margin of around 10.5%, which it describes as the low end of its previously stated 10.5% to 11% range, and operating cash flow of around $1.2 billion.

Gentex reported net sales of $647.7 million versus $655.2 million, down 1.1% by our calculation. GAAP net income attributable to the company was $90.6 million versus $101.0 million, and diluted EPS was $0.43 versus $0.46, while adjusted diluted EPS was flat at $0.47. Gross margin was 33.4% versus 34.4%, which Gentex attributed to higher precious metal costs and lower-than-anticipated sales. It now expects 2026 consolidated revenue of approximately $2.65 billion, versus $2.65 billion to $2.75 billion before, and gross margin of 34.0% to 34.5%, versus 34.5% to 35.5%. The company repurchased 5.7 million shares for $132.6 million in the quarter.

The Federal Home Loan Bank of Atlanta reported preliminary third-quarter net income of $126 million versus $155 million, a decline of 18.7% by our calculation. Total assets were $166.7 billion at Sept. 30 versus $146.2 billion at Dec. 31, 2025, up 14.0%, and period-end advances were $105.2 billion versus $95.0 billion, up 10.8%. Average advances, however, were $95.2 billion in the quarter versus $102.8 billion a year earlier. The board approved an annualized dividend rate of 6.20 percent, to be credited on Oct. 27, and retained earnings stood at $3.1 billion. The figures are approximate until the Form 10-Q, expected on or about Nov. 5.

Orchid Island Capital reported a net loss of $178.9 million, or $(0.90) per share, against net income of $72.1 million, or $0.53 per share, in the third quarter of 2025. Book value per share was $6.02 at Sept. 30, and dividends declared were $0.30 per share versus $0.36 a year earlier.

None of these releases gave a single common explanation, and each company's own statements should be read on their own terms. The practical takeaway from the day is narrower: in the auto-parts reports, cost and mix language did more work than demand language, and in the mortgage-linked reports, the balance sheet and the income statement told different stories in the same quarter. We will keep tracking company guidance and official data as the week of Oct. 26 begins.

items.title: Guidance splits: AmEx and Danaher raise, Gentex trims, American guides to a loss
items.dek: Companies that raised 2026 outlooks cited demand and cash flow; those that cut or warned cited metal and fuel costs.
key_points: American Express: 2026 EPS guidance $18.30-$18.60 ($17.60-$17.90 adjusted); Q3 billed business $454.0B vs. $421.0B.
Danaher: 2026 adjusted EPS guidance $8.57-$8.62 vs. $8.45-$8.60 before; Q3 core sales +3.0%.
Gentex: 2026 revenue approximately $2.65B vs. $2.65B-$2.75B before; gross margin 34.0%-34.5% vs. 34.5%-35.5%.
American Airlines: Q3 fuel expense $4,635M vs. $2,767M; Q4 adjusted loss per share guided to $(1.10) to $(0.50).
body: Four companies that reported between Oct. 21 and Oct. 23 gave updated outlooks that point in different directions, and the useful comparison is what each one said is driving its range: demand, mix, input costs or fuel.

American Express guided 2026 diluted EPS to $18.30 to $18.60, or $17.60 to $17.90 on an adjusted basis. Against $15.38 in 2025, that is roughly 19% to 21% on a GAAP basis by our arithmetic. The release reports Q3 billed business of $454.0 billion versus $421.0 billion, up 8%, and a credit provision of $1.0 billion versus $1.3 billion, which it ties to a reserve release this quarter against a reserve build last year. The reported EPS of $5.42 includes a gain tied to GBTG, so the adjusted $4.68 is the cleaner base.

Danaher raised 2026 adjusted EPS guidance to $8.57 to $8.62 from $8.45 to $8.60. The low end rose $0.12 and the high end $0.02, so the range tightened from $0.15 wide to $0.05 wide. Core sales grew 3.0% in the quarter, or 5.5% excluding respiratory testing, and free cash flow was $1,632 million versus $1,370 million.

body.h: A trim and a loss forecast

body: Gentex now expects 2026 revenue of approximately $2.65 billion, where it previously guided $2.65 billion to $2.75 billion, and gross margin of 34.0% to 34.5% versus 34.5% to 35.5%. Q3 gross margin was 33.4% versus 34.4%, which the company attributed mainly to higher precious metal costs and lower-than-expected sales. Its 2027 revenue outlook of $2.80 billion to $2.90 billion was maintained and assumes primary-market light vehicle production declines about 1%.

American Airlines reported Q3 revenue of $16,335 million, up 19.3%, but fuel expense of $4,635 million versus $2,767 million. By our arithmetic fuel was about 28% of revenue versus about 20% a year earlier. The company guides a Q4 adjusted loss per share of $(1.10) to $(0.50) and a full-year loss of $(1.60) to $(1.00), assuming fuel of about $4.70 per gallon in Q4.

The two raises came from companies whose releases cite spending volume and cash generation. The two cautious outlooks cite input costs: precious metals at Gentex and fuel at American. The ranges also differ in width. Danaher narrowed to a $0.05 band, while American's Q4 range spans $0.60, a reminder that guidance ranges are widest where a single price drives results.

These are company statements about their own outlooks, not forecasts by AlphaGen. The pattern worth tracking in the next round of reports is whether input-cost language, rather than demand language, keeps appearing in the cautious outlooks.

items.title: Morning Brief: Mortgage rates ease to 7.32% as bank earnings arrive and FOMC week nears
items.dek: A thin official calendar leaves rates and corporate results in focus, with the Fed, GDP and PCE data, and three Treasury note auctions next week.
key_points: BEA lists only GDP (advance, Q3) and Personal Income and Outlays (Sept) between today and Oct. 30, both 8:30 a.m. ET Oct. 29; the Fed calendar shows no FOMC events or speeches today.
Freddie Mac: the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaged 7.32% as of Oct. 22, down from 7.40% a week earlier and 6.19% a year ago; the 15-year was 6.68%.
10-year Treasury yield was 5.13% on Oct. 21, versus 5.12% on Oct. 20 and 5.09% on Oct. 16 (Federal Reserve H.15 via FRED).
Earnings: First Citizens Q3 net income $606M (new $1.2B repurchase plan); Flagstar provision $76M versus $18M in Q2; Rithm Capital reports before the NYSE open, call at 8:00 a.m. ET.
Next week: FOMC Oct. 27-28 (press conference Oct. 28, 2:30 p.m. ET); Treasury 2-, 5- and 7-year note auctions on Oct. 26, 27 and 29.
talking_points: Mortgage rates averaged 7.32% last week, down slightly from 7.40% the week before, but still well above the 6.19% of a year ago, so borrowing costs for homebuyers remain a real hurdle.
The 10-year Treasury yield was 5.13% on October 21, and because mortgage rates tend to track long-term Treasury yields, that benchmark is a useful gauge of what home financing may cost.
First Citizens announced a plan to buy back up to $1.2 billion of its shares through 2027, a reminder that banks weigh returning capital to shareholders alongside lending to customers.
body: Friday's official calendar is thin. The Bureau of Economic Analysis lists only two releases between today and October 30, GDP (advance estimate) for the third quarter and Personal Income and Outlays for September, both at 8:30 a.m. ET on October 29. The Federal Reserve Board's calendar for today shows no speeches or FOMC events, with the commercial paper release at 1:00 p.m. and the H.8 and H.15 statistical releases at 4:15 p.m. ET.

The clearest rate datapoint arrived yesterday. Freddie Mac's survey showed the 30-year fixed mortgage rate averaging 7.32% as of October 22, down from 7.40% a week earlier and 6.19% a year ago. The 15-year rate was 6.68%, versus 6.71% a week earlier and 5.44% a year ago. FRED shows the 30-year series at 7.03% on September 24 and 7.28% on October 1, so the latest reading is lower than the past two weeks but higher than late September.

Treasury yields remain the backdrop. The 10-year constant maturity yield was 5.13% on October 21, versus 5.12% on October 20 and 5.09% on October 16, according to the Federal Reserve's H.15 data on FRED. The October 22 observation had not yet been published when this note was written. Our Chart of the Day looks at how the mortgage rate and the 10-year yield have moved together.

Earnings flow continues. First Citizens BancShares reported third-quarter net income of $606 million versus $672 million in the second quarter, and announced a repurchase plan of up to $1.2 billion through 2027. Flagstar Bank's provision for credit losses was $76 million versus $18 million in the second quarter. Rogers Communications reported revenue of C$5,443 million versus C$5,348 million, and Balchem reported net sales of $290.7 million, up 8.6%. Rithm Capital said it will release results before the New York Stock Exchange opens today, with its call at 8:00 a.m. ET.

Overseas, the Statistics Bureau of Japan's schedule lists the national September consumer price index for today, October 23. We have not yet read the figures from the Bureau, so we make no statement about the result here.

Looking ahead, the Federal Open Market Committee meets October 27-28, with a press conference at 2:30 p.m. ET on October 28. Treasury's tentative auction schedule lists 2-year notes on Monday, October 26, 5-year notes on Tuesday, October 27 and 7-year notes on Thursday, October 29. Those auctions, the FOMC decision and the GDP and PCE data on October 29 make next week the busiest of the month for rates.

items.title: The Close: Fuel costs and capex weigh on results as central banks diverge
items.dek: Union Pacific and Liberty Energy reported fuel and capital-spending pressure, while Korea held rates and Turkey cut.
key_points: Union Pacific: fuel unfavorably affected the Q3 operating ratio by 140 basis points; Q3 revenue was $7,197M, up 15%, and diluted EPS was $3.49 versus $3.01.
Liberty Energy: Q3 revenue rose 26.3% to $1,196.2M, but it posted a $39.1M net loss as capex reached $621.9M versus $113.0M.
Lazard: Q3 GAAP net revenue was $814M versus $748M, yet GAAP diluted EPS fell to $0.26 from $0.65.
Bank of Korea held its Base Rate at 3.00% on a 7-0 vote; Turkey's central bank cut its one-week repo rate to 36% from 37%.
talking_points: Union Pacific said higher fuel prices hurt its operating ratio by 140 basis points this quarter, a reminder that energy costs can squeeze profit margins even when revenue and shipping volumes are growing.
Liberty Energy's revenue grew 26% but it posted a loss after spending $621.9 million on equipment, showing that companies investing heavily for future demand can see current earnings fall first.
The Bank of Korea held rates at 3.00% while Turkey's central bank cut to 36%, so central banks worldwide are moving in different directions, and everyday investors should not assume one path for all.
body: Thursday's results were a study in how input costs and investment spending can separate revenue growth from profit growth, while two central banks took different steps on the same day.

Union Pacific reported third-quarter operating revenue of $7,197 million versus $6,244 million a year earlier, up 15.3% by our calculation. Operating income rose to $2,943 million from $2,549 million. Reported diluted EPS was $3.49 versus $3.01, and adjusted diluted EPS was $3.53 versus $3.08. Revenue carloads grew 6%. The company said higher fuel prices unfavorably affected its operating ratio by 140 basis points, and that its reported 2026 operating ratio is challenged by high fuel prices while the core business is improving. It affirmed high-single-digit reported EPS growth for 2026 and listed a $3.5 billion capital plan as updated.

Liberty Energy shows the other side of heavy investment. Its revenue was $1,196.2 million versus $947.4 million a year earlier, up 26.3%, and adjusted EBITDA was $141.6 million. But it reported a net loss of $39.1 million, or $(0.24) per diluted share, against net income of $43.1 million, or $0.26. Capital expenditures were $621.9 million versus $113.0 million. The company also described a strategic development agreement covering 1.2 GW of integrated power services at data center campuses, with a first energy service agreement of about 500 MW targeted by December 2026 and phased energization from Q4 2027 through Q1 2029. It declared a $0.10 quarterly dividend, up from $0.09.

Lazard reported GAAP net revenue of $814 million versus $748 million, up 8.8%. Financial Advisory revenue was $470 million versus $427 million, and Asset Management revenue was $357 million versus $327 million. Even so, GAAP diluted EPS fell to $0.26 from $0.65, and adjusted diluted EPS to $0.36 from $0.56. The company repurchased $33 million of stock in the quarter. East West Bancorp, which reported earlier in the week, posted Q3 net income of $382 million versus $368 million and diluted EPS of $2.76 versus $2.65.

The Bank of Korea held its Base Rate at 3.00% on Oct. 22, with all seven board members voting for the hold. It reported September consumer price inflation of 2.9% and core inflation of 2.8%, and said it will decide the timing and pace of further increases after reviewing third-quarter GDP and October inflation data. The Central Bank of the Republic of Turkiye moved the other way, lowering its one-week repo auction rate by 1 percentage point to 36%. It said recent figures confirm a deceleration in underlying inflation, while flagging elevated energy prices as an upside risk.

Fuel is the common thread between the railroad's margin comment and the Turkish committee's inflation warning. In the United States, the next official events are the Federal Open Market Committee meeting on Oct. 27-28 and the advance third-quarter GDP and September PCE releases on Oct. 29, according to the schedule cited in this morning's brief.

items.title: Organic growth splits Allegion, Philip Morris and Snap-on
items.dek: Allegion and Philip Morris grew organic sales by more than 7%; Snap-on's organic sales fell 2.8%.
key_points: Allegion: Q3 revenue $1,172.6M (+9.6%), organic +7.2%; 2026 organic growth guided to 5.0%-6.0%.
Philip Morris International: Q3 net revenues $11,438M (+5.5%, +7.1% organic); full-year adjusted EPS forecast $8.29-$8.44.
Snap-on: Q3 net sales $1,183.7M (-0.6%), organic sales -2.8%; diluted EPS $4.64 vs. $5.02, with a $0.31 legal settlement benefit in the year-ago quarter.
Reported EPS diverged from adjusted at Philip Morris: $2.12 (-4.9%) vs. $2.36 (+5.4%).
body: Three U.S. companies that sell very different products reported third-quarter results on Oct. 21 and 22, and the most useful comparison is not profit but how much of each company's sales growth came from underlying volume and pricing rather than acquisitions or currency.

Allegion, which makes locks and access hardware, reported revenue of $1,172.6 million versus $1,070.2 million a year earlier, up 9.6%, with organic growth of 7.2%. Philip Morris International reported net revenues of $11,438 million versus $10,845 million, up 5.5% reported and 7.1% organically. Snap-on moved the other way: net sales were $1,183.7 million versus $1,190.8 million, a 0.6% decline, with organic sales down 2.8% and acquisitions adding $25.6 million.

Reported and organic growth diverge in both directions. At Allegion the reported rate was 2.4 percentage points above the organic one, and at Philip Morris it was 1.6 points below. The release passages we read do not break those gaps down, so we do not attribute them. At Snap-on, acquisitions are what kept reported sales close to flat.

body.h: Earnings per share tell a more mixed story

body: Allegion's reported diluted EPS rose to $2.59 from $2.18, and adjusted EPS rose to $2.60 from $2.30. Philip Morris reported diluted EPS of $2.12, down 4.9% from $2.23, while adjusted diluted EPS grew 5.4% to $2.36 from $2.24. Snap-on's diluted EPS fell to $4.64 from $5.02, a 7.6% decline.

The Snap-on comparison needs care. The year-ago quarter included a $22.0 million operating benefit from the settlement of a legal matter, worth $0.31 per diluted share after tax, according to the release. By our arithmetic, removing that $0.31 puts the prior-year figure at $4.71, so the underlying decline is smaller than the headline one, though still a decline. Operating earnings before financial services were $248.1 million, or 21.0% of net sales, versus $278.5 million, or 23.4%. The release says the prior-year benefit was 190 basis points of that margin.

Allegion guided 2026 adjusted EPS to $9.05 to $9.10 and organic revenue growth to 5.0% to 6.0%. The 7.2% organic growth in the quarter is above the top of that annual range. Philip Morris guided full-year adjusted diluted EPS to $8.29 to $8.44, up 9.9% to 11.9% from $7.54 in 2025, and said the update was for currency only. It also said organic operating income growth of 7% to 9% is now more likely to land in the middle or lower half of the range.

Reported growth can be assembled from acquisitions and currency, which is why organic figures are the cleaner read on demand. On that measure, this week's three reports show two companies growing underlying sales at more than 7% and one shrinking, and a one-time item from last year complicating the earnings comparison for the third. Investors comparing these companies should look past the headline growth rate to the organic line and the prior-year adjustments.

items.title: Morning Brief: A light data day as Lockheed and Quest lift 2026 outlooks

items.title: Aerospace and defense: backlogs are growing faster than sales
items.dek: RTX, GE Aerospace and Northrop Grumman all raised 2026 guidance on Oct. 20, and all three are booking demand faster than they can ship it.
key_points: RTX: Q3 sales $24.97B (+12% organic), backlog $340B; 2026 adjusted EPS outlook raised to $7.65-$7.75 from $7.10-$7.25.
GE Aerospace: Q3 orders $19.0B (+49%) vs. adjusted revenue $13.29B (+18%); 2026 adjusted EPS guide raised to $8.00-$8.10.
Northrop Grumman: backlog $109.6B at Sept. 30, up from $95.7B at end-2025; 2026 MTM-adjusted EPS guide raised to $29.35-$29.75.
Cash lagged at two of three: RTX Q3 free cash flow $2.12B vs. $4.03B a year earlier; GE $2.04B vs. $2.36B.
body: Three major U.S. aerospace and defense companies reported on Oct. 20, and the common thread was not the quarter itself but the order book behind it. RTX, GE Aerospace and Northrop Grumman each raised full-year guidance, and each is taking in demand faster than it is converting that demand to revenue.

GE Aerospace reported third-quarter orders of $19.0 billion, up 49%, against adjusted revenue of $13.29 billion, up 18%. RTX ended the quarter with a $340 billion backlog after 12% organic sales growth. Northrop Grumman's backlog rose to $109.6 billion at Sept. 30 from $95.7 billion at the end of 2025, a $13.9 billion build in nine months on quarterly sales of $11.12 billion.

When orders grow roughly two to three times faster than revenue, as at GE, the constraint on growth shifts from demand to capacity: supply chains, labor and factory throughput. That is a better problem than weak demand, but it means near-term results depend on execution more than on new wins.

body.h: Guidance moved up across the board

body: RTX raised its 2026 adjusted sales outlook to $97.0-$97.5 billion from $95.0-$96.0 billion, organic growth to 10%-11% from 8%-9%, and adjusted EPS to $7.65-$7.75 from $7.10-$7.25. GE Aerospace lifted adjusted EPS guidance to $8.00-$8.10 from $7.65-$7.85 and operating profit to $10.9-$11.0 billion. Northrop moved MTM-adjusted EPS guidance to $29.35-$29.75 from $28.60-$29.10.

Cash flow was the weaker line. RTX's third-quarter free cash flow was $2.12 billion versus $4.03 billion a year earlier, and GE Aerospace's was $2.04 billion versus $2.36 billion, even as both raised full-year free cash flow ranges. Northrop went the other way, with adjusted free cash flow of $1.81 billion versus $1.26 billion.

The AlphaGen read: the sector's earnings story for 2026 is now about converting large order books into deliveries. The guidance raises show management confidence in that conversion; the uneven quarterly cash numbers are the place to watch for whether production is keeping pace.

items.title: Fed plumbing: Treasury's cash account, not QT, is now moving reserves
items.dek: With the Fed's balance sheet flat and its reverse repo facility nearly empty, swings in Treasury's cash balance are passing straight through to bank reserves.
key_points: Fed total assets were $6,755.6 billion on Oct. 14, up $8.1 billion on the week and about $9 billion above their Sept. 16 level.
Reserve balances averaged $3,022.1 billion in the week ended Oct. 14, $91.9 billion above the week ended Sept. 23.
The Treasury General Account averaged $883.4 billion, down $93.7 billion from $977.1 billion in the week ended Sept. 23.
Overnight reverse repo usage was $1.201 billion on Oct. 15, and SOFR was 3.88% on Oct. 14 versus a 3.90% interest rate on reserve balances.
body: The Federal Reserve's weekly balance sheet has gone quiet. Total assets were $6,755.6 billion on Wednesday, Oct. 14, up $8.1 billion from a week earlier and only about $9 billion above the Sept. 16 reading of $6,746.5 billion, according to H.4.1 data on FRED. Over five weeks the Fed's footprint has barely moved.

Bank reserves have not been nearly as calm. Reserve balances averaged $3,022.1 billion in the week ended Oct. 14, down $7.5 billion on the week. But they had averaged $2,930.2 billion in the week ended Sept. 23 and $3,013.8 billion in the week ended Sept. 16, a swing of more than $80 billion in each direction within a month.

body.h: Treasury's account is the swing factor

body: The mirror image sits in the Treasury General Account, the government's checking account at the Fed. It averaged $877.0 billion in the week ended Sept. 16, jumped to $977.1 billion in the week ended Sept. 23, and has since fallen back to $883.4 billion. The $93.7 billion decline since late September lines up closely with the $91.9 billion rise in reserves over the same span. The September spike coincided with the mid-month corporate tax date, when receipts flow into Treasury's account and drain cash from the banking system.

In earlier years, money-market funds could absorb such swings by moving cash in and out of the Fed's overnight reverse repo facility. That buffer is effectively gone: usage was $1.201 billion on Oct. 15 and $0.201 billion on Oct. 14. Every dollar Treasury now pulls into its account comes out of reserves, and every dollar it spends goes back in.

body.h: No strain yet in funding rates

body: So far the money markets are taking this in stride. The Secured Overnight Financing Rate was 3.88% on Oct. 14, 2 basis points below the 3.90% interest rate on reserve balances. Repo trading at or above the reserve rate has historically been the signal that reserves are getting scarce; that signal is not flashing today.

Reserves near $3 trillion look ample for now, but the system has lost its shock absorber. That makes Treasury's cash-management choices, including how much it holds in the TGA around tax dates, quarter-ends and heavy bill settlements, the main source of week-to-week liquidity volatility. The spread between SOFR and the reserve rate is the simplest gauge to watch: if repo starts printing above 3.90% around the next tax or settlement date, the debate over whether reserves are still ample will return quickly.

body: Friday's earnings slate is all regional banks, and it splits two ways. Citizens, Regions and M&T delivered straightforward quarters built on margins and lower credit losses. Truist, like First Horizon on Thursday, used the quarter to take losses now in exchange for a better earnings base later.

Truist reported diluted EPS of $0.56 versus $1.04 a year earlier. The gap to its $1.16 adjusted figure comes from a $1.4 billion pretax loss on AFS securities sales ($0.90 a share), a $581 million reserve recapture (a $0.36 benefit) and $0.06 of impacts tied to selling Regional Acceptance Corporation loans. The RAC sale accounted for $5.5 billion of a $5.9 billion drop in loans held for investment and lifted the net charge-off ratio to 0.77%, 39 basis points of it from RAC. The bank still bought back $1.2 billion of stock, leaving preliminary CET1 at 10.7%.

Citizens' net interest income rose to $1,675 million from $1,488 million and its margin widened to 3.18% from 2.99%, lifting EPS to $1.41 from $1.05. Regions earned $0.71 a share with a 3.68% margin and net charge-offs of 0.29% of loans, down from 0.55% a year ago. M&T's EPS rose to $5.04 from $4.82 even though net income slipped to $775 million, as buybacks shrank the share count and estimated CET1 fell to 10.16% from 10.99%. The common thread is that credit costs are falling while margins hold, which is the opposite of what an energy-driven slowdown would normally produce for lenders.

BLS publishes September import and export prices at 8:30 a.m. ET, and the Fed's industrial production report follows at 9:15 a.m. After this week's producer-price data, the import figures will show how much of the energy shock is arriving through traded goods. In Europe, Eurostat's final data put September inflation at 3.8%, with energy up 18.9% on the year and adding 1.71 percentage points; services inflation edged up to 3.2% from 3.0%, the component most sensitive to ECB policy.

items.dek: Interactive Brokers, J.B. Hunt and Alcoa capped a heavy reporting day, while the Fed's H.15 shows the 2-year yield rising as the long end eased.

body: Thursday's reporting day ended with three after-the-bell releases that each tell a different part of the economy's story: a broker living on interest income, a freight carrier moving more boxes for thinner margins, and an aluminum producer coming off a strong second quarter. They followed this morning's producer price and retail sales reports, covered earlier on the wire, and a TSMC report that set the tone for technology.

Customer accounts rose 35% to 5.58 million, customer equity 27% to $964.7 billion, and margin loans 36% to $105.2 billion. The board lifted the quarterly dividend to $0.15 from $0.0875.

Freight demand is not the problem; cost and pricing are.

Revenue of $3,704 million was well above the $2,995 million of a year ago but below $3,966 million in the second quarter, and adjusted EBITDA excluding special items slipped to $789 million from $901 million. The company reaffirmed 2026 aluminum production of 2.4 to 2.6 million metric tons.

Interest-rich and pricing-power businesses are capturing it; asset-heavy operators facing fuel and labor costs are not. Import prices and industrial production are due Friday morning.

items.title: Crop protection's reset: FMC reprices the channel as Corteva fights in court
items.dek: FMC's guidance cut and Corteva's legal fight over its split show the crop-input business working through price deflation and governance risk at the same time.
key_points: FMC now guides Q3 revenue to $65 million–$125 million and adjusted EBITDA to negative $565 million–$510 million, versus July guidance of $840 million–$900 million and $120 million–$140 million.
The cut includes a $625 million–$675 million impact from lowering prices on FMC products held by channel customers in Brazil, Argentina, the U.S. and Canada.
FMC said a triggering event for intangible impairment testing occurred as of Sept. 30 and that it plans to discuss further covenant modifications with its bank group.
Corteva disclosed a temporary restraining order, now stayed pending a Seventh Circuit motion, that would bar dividends and buybacks after its Oct. 1 separation from Vylor.
body: Two filings this week put the crop-protection industry back in focus. FMC slashed its third-quarter outlook to reprice products sitting in distributor warehouses, and Corteva disclosed that a multistate lawsuit over its newly completed separation has produced a court order restricting capital returns. One is a pricing problem and the other a legal one, but both land on the same theme: the economics of branded crop chemicals are under pressure.

body.h: FMC: taking the hit up front

body: FMC now expects third-quarter revenue of $65 million to $125 million and adjusted EBITDA of negative $565 million to negative $510 million. In July it had guided to $840 million to $900 million of revenue excluding India and $120 million to $140 million of adjusted EBITDA. The difference is mostly deliberate: the estimates include a $625 million to $675 million impact from commercial actions, chiefly cutting prices on products already held by channel customers in Brazil, Argentina, the U.S. and Canada, and narrowing the gap between gross and net pricing in the U.S., where the company has historically paired high list prices with high rebates.

FMC said "third-quarter demand was weaker than we expected," and the company pointed to rapid price declines, partly from increased generic competition, that widened the gap between the value of channel inventory and current market prices. FMC also said distributors are running their lowest inventory levels in its history. In its July release, the company had already reported second-quarter revenue of $867.1 million, down from $1,050.5 million a year earlier, and expected full-year price to be lower by mid-to-high single digits.

The balance sheet is the pressure point. FMC said a triggering event for intangible impairment testing occurred as of Sept. 30 and that it may record a material non-cash charge. It expects to comply with covenants at quarter-end but plans to talk with its bank group about further covenant modifications over the next year. Total debt was $4.28 billion at June 30.

body.h: Corteva: the split is done, the payout is frozen

body: Corteva completed its separation from Vylor on Oct. 1, the same day 15 states and one sovereign sued in federal court in Indiana to challenge it. On Oct. 9 the court issued a temporary restraining order barring the companies from paying dividends, repurchasing stock or disposing of assets outside the ordinary course. The court stayed that order on Oct. 10 pending an emergency motion at the Seventh Circuit, relying on Corteva's representation that it does not intend to declare dividends or repurchase shares while the motion is pending. Corteva said it strongly contests the claims.

FMC's reset reads as a company choosing one very bad quarter over several mediocre ones, and cleaner channel pricing could make future results easier to read. The risk is that the impairment and covenant talks crystallize just as generic pressure persists. For Corteva, the separation itself is not unwound, but shareholders face an uncertain wait on capital returns. FMC's Oct. 29 results and Oct. 30 call, where it plans to share preliminary 2027 and 2028 expectations, are the next checkpoints.

items.title: Beyond the banks: margins, warehouses and temp workers point to a sturdier real economy
items.dek: UnitedHealth, Prologis and ManpowerGroup add non-financial evidence to a week dominated by bank results and an energy-driven inflation shock.
key_points: UnitedHealth Q3 adjusted EPS rose to $4.69 from $2.92 as its medical care ratio fell to 88.4% from 89.9%, even as revenues slipped to $112.69 billion.
Prologis lifted the midpoint of 2026 core FFO guidance to $6.25–$6.29 after signing 60 million square feet of leases at 95.1% average occupancy.
ManpowerGroup revenue grew 5.2% in constant currency to $4.84 billion, and management cited improving demand.
Initial jobless claims were 199,000 in the week ending Oct. 10, with the four-week average at 198,500.
body: Third-quarter earnings so far have mostly been a bank story. Three non-bank reports this week offer a read on the real economy from different angles: health care costs, logistics space and temporary hiring. Together they describe an economy that is absorbing the energy shock without a demand break, which is the backdrop the Fed is weighing against producer and consumer price data running hot.

body.h: Health care: margin repair, not growth

body: UnitedHealth reported Q3 revenues of $112.694 billion versus $113.161 billion a year earlier, and UnitedHealthcare served 48.3 million people versus 50.1 million. Profitability moved the other way: diluted EPS rose to $4.56 from $2.59, adjusted EPS to $4.69 from $2.92, and the medical care ratio improved to 88.4% from 89.9%. The company raised its 2026 outlook to at least $19.50 of EPS and at least $20.50 adjusted. Our read is that this is a pricing and cost-discipline recovery, not a volume one, and that medical cost trends are no longer worsening faster than premiums.

Prologis reported core FFO of $1.60 per share versus $1.49 and total revenues of $2.388 billion versus $2.214 billion. Average occupancy was 95.1% and period-end occupancy 95.6%, and net effective rent change on its share of leases was 38.0%. CEO Daniel S. Letter said customers "are running lean on inventory, and excess capacity within their networks has largely cleared." Core FFO guidance moved to $6.25–$6.29 from $6.22–$6.30, while the net EPS range was cut to $4.05–$4.15. Lean inventories with little spare space is a configuration where any restocking shows up quickly in leasing.

body.h: Labor: still tight at the margin

body: ManpowerGroup reported Q3 revenues of $4.84 billion versus $4.63 billion, up 5.2% in constant currency, and guided Q4 diluted EPS to $1.03–$1.13. Staffing demand tends to turn before payrolls do, so growth here is a useful counterpoint to fears that energy costs are already forcing cuts. Thursday's claims report fits: initial claims of 199,000 and insured unemployment of 1.71 million show few layoffs.

None of these reports says the energy shock is harmless; it says the economy is carrying it so far. That keeps the policy debate centered on inflation pass-through rather than on growth support, and it raises the bar for any data that would argue the other way.

items.title: September PPI: the energy shock moves up the pipeline
items.dek: Producer prices posted their biggest monthly gain since March 2022, and upstream costs are rising far faster than consumer core inflation.
key_points: Final demand PPI rose 1.3% in September, seasonally adjusted, after 0.5% in August, and 6.3% over 12 months unadjusted.
Energy rose 10.8%; gasoline, up 20.3%, accounted for half of the 2.6% rise in goods prices.
Final demand less foods, energy and trade services rose 0.5% on the month and 5.0% on the year.
Unprocessed intermediate goods prices rose 21.5% over 12 months; processed goods rose 14.1%.
Core CPI rose 2.6% over the year to September, and China's PPI rose 5.0% against 0.9% consumer inflation.
body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics' September Producer Price Index confirms that the energy shock visible in Wednesday's CPI is at least as large one step up the supply chain. Final demand prices rose 1.3% in the month, seasonally adjusted, the largest advance since a 1.7% gain in March 2022, after increases of 0.5% in August and 0.2% in July. On an unadjusted basis, final demand prices were up 6.3% from a year earlier.

Goods prices rose 2.6%, and the energy index jumped 10.8%. BLS traces half of the goods increase to gasoline, which rose 20.3%. Food prices rose 1.2%, while goods excluding food and energy rose a more modest 0.3%. On the services side, the 0.8% gain came largely from a 1.4% rise in trade margins, while transportation and warehousing prices rose 3.4% as fuel costs moved into freight.

The intermediate-demand indexes show how much cost pressure is still working its way through. Processed goods for intermediate demand rose 2.5% in September and 14.1% over 12 months. Unprocessed goods rose 8.4% in the month and 21.5% over the year. Intermediate services rose 0.9% and 6.3%.
BLS's narrower core measure, final demand less foods, energy and trade services, rose 0.5% in September and 5.0% over 12 months.

Compare that with the consumer side. BLS reported Wednesday that the CPI rose 3.7% over the 12 months ending September, and the index excluding food and energy rose 2.6%. Producer-level core inflation is running about twice the consumer-level core rate. That gap is either being absorbed in margins or has yet to reach shelves.

The same pattern shows up abroad. China's National Bureau of Statistics reported that producer prices rose 5.0% from a year earlier in September, up from 3.8% in August, while consumer prices rose just 0.9%.

Markets are not yet pricing in much pass-through. The 10-year breakeven inflation rate on FRED stood at 2.35% on October 14. If trade margins keep widening and transport costs keep climbing, the pass-through from producer to consumer prices will matter more for the Fed's next steps than any single month's headline. The next PPI release is scheduled for November 13.

items.title: Beige Book: the oil shock is everywhere, demand is not
items.dek: Every District reported higher oil prices feeding costs, while consumer spending was flat and growth mostly slight. That mix shapes the pace of the Fed's tightening.
key_points: Two of 12 Districts reported moderate growth, three modest, four slight and three no significant change, per the October Beige Book (information through Oct. 5).
"Higher oil prices permeated all District reports"; four Districts said price increases accelerated, three called price growth robust and eight moderate.
Most Districts saw little or no change in consumer spending, and over half said it was driven by high-income households.
Governor Waller said 16 of 18 dot submitters anticipated at least one more hike after September's move to 3.75%–4%, but hikes need not come at consecutive meetings.
PNC's Q3 release assumes two more Fed hikes, taking the fed funds rate to 4.25%–4.50%.
body: The Fed's October Beige Book, compiled by the Philadelphia Fed from information collected on or before Oct. 5, describes an economy that is barely growing while its cost base is rising. Two of the 12 Districts reported moderate growth, three modest growth, four slight growth and three no significant change.

The prices section states flatly: "Higher oil prices permeated all District reports." Four Districts said the pace of price increases picked up since the prior report, three described overall price growth as robust and eight as moderate. Contacts flagged diesel costs and fuel surcharges moving through supply chains, along with continued pressure from other commodities, tariffs and insurance, and firms in several Districts expect prices to rise further as contracts expire and hedges are renegotiated.

The demand side is the counterweight. Most Districts reported little or no change in consumer spending, and over half said spending was driven by high-income households. Consumer-facing firms reported tighter margins as price-sensitive customers resist increases. Labor market conditions were little changed, labor supply was generally adequate, and five Districts said some firms trimmed staffing through attrition or delayed hiring after investing in AI.

That combination lands on a committee already in tightening mode. In an Oct. 8 speech, Governor Waller noted the FOMC raised its policy rate 25 basis points in September to 3.75%–4%, that 16 of the 18 participants who submitted dots anticipated at least one more hike, and that the hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings. He said that for at least the near term, policy will be focused on the inflation side of the mandate. Banks are planning around the same path: PNC's third-quarter release assumes two more hikes that take the fed funds rate to 4.25%–4.50%.

The Beige Book argues for patience as much as for action. Energy is clearly reaching business costs, but flat consumer spending and margin compression suggest firms have limited ability to pass it all on, which caps how far second-round inflation can run. That is the case for Waller's non-consecutive framing: the committee can keep a hiking bias without moving at the Oct. 27–28 meeting if pass-through stalls. The risk is the forward-looking line on contracts and hedges, which says more of the oil shock is still in the pipeline. We would watch the October CPI on Nov. 10 for evidence that fuel costs are spreading into core goods and services.

items.title: Fannie Mae's new forecast pushes mortgage relief past 2027
items.dek: One month after projecting rates near 6.7%, Fannie Mae's economists now see 7.5% next year and fewer home sales.
key_points: Fannie Mae's Oct. 12 forecast sees the 30-year fixed rate averaging 7.4% in 4Q26 and 7.5% in 2027, versus 6.8% and 6.7% in the Sept. 11 forecast.
The 2027 total home sales forecast was cut to 4.713 million from 4.882 million, and existing-home sales to 4.061 million from 4.215 million.
Projected 2027 housing starts were trimmed to 1.301 million from 1.327 million.
Fannie Mae's home price forecast for 2026 rose to 2.7% from 2.3%, while 2027 was cut to 0.6% from 1.0%.
body: Fannie Mae's Economic and Strategic Research group publishes a housing forecast every month, and the October edition, dated Oct. 12, marks a sharp break from September. The group now expects the 30-year fixed mortgage rate to average 7.4% in the fourth quarter of 2026 and 7.5% in every quarter of 2027. In its Sept. 11 forecast, the same quarters were pencilled in at 6.8% and 6.7%.

The revision changes the shape of the path, not just its level. September's forecast had rates easing slightly into 2027 and then holding flat at 6.7%; October's has them stepping up and staying there. For full-year 2026 the average moves to 6.7% from 6.5%, which implies most of the change is concentrated in the final quarter and beyond. Fannie Mae's tables do not attribute the shift to a single cause, but the timing coincides with the energy-driven jump in inflation and a long end of the Treasury curve that has repriced higher.

Higher rates feed straight into turnover. Fannie Mae cut its 2027 total home sales forecast to 4.713 million from 4.882 million, a reduction of 169,000, or about 3.5% by our calculation. Existing-home sales for 2027 were lowered to 4.061 million from 4.215 million. The 2026 total moved down to 4.672 million from 4.692 million, so this year is largely locked in and the damage falls on next year.

Construction is not spared. Total housing starts are now seen at 1.341 million in 2026 and 1.301 million in 2027, down from 1.351 million and 1.327 million. Fewer starts in a forecast that also expects slower price growth points to builders pulling back rather than chasing volume.

The price outlook splits in two. Fannie Mae raised its 2026 home price growth forecast to 2.7% from 2.3%, consistent with tight inventory as owners with low locked-in rates stay put. But it cut 2027 growth to 0.6% from 1.0%. That is the lock-in effect at work: supply stays scarce enough to hold prices up in the near term, while affordability eventually caps them.

The October forecast is a meaningful signal because it comes from one of the two government-sponsored mortgage enterprises, and it moves in the opposite direction from a month ago. If rates track this path, the housing market faces another year of low turnover, which weighs on mortgage originators, brokerages and home-improvement demand tied to moves. The key swing factor is the 10-year Treasury yield: any relief there would likely show up quickly in mortgage rates, but Fannie Mae is no longer assuming it.

items.title: EIA's October outlook: oil supply is healing, inventories are not
items.dek: The Energy Information Administration sees Brent easing from a $114 September to $105 in the fourth quarter, but its own numbers show global stocks still drawing and diesel still tight.
key_points: EIA forecasts Brent at $105 per barrel in 4Q26, $96 for 2026 and $84 for 2027, after a September average of $114, $23 above August.
Middle East shut-in production averaged 4.8 million b/d in September, down from a 10.9 million b/d peak in May; EIA forecasts 4.5 million b/d in 4Q26.
EIA estimates global oil inventories fell by an average of 1.9 million b/d in 3Q26 and expects a further draw of about 0.7 million b/d in 4Q26.
East Coast distillate inventories were 32% below the five-year seasonal average in September; EIA expects them to stay about 20% below average through winter.
Retail diesel is forecast at $5.19 a gallon in 2026 and $4.49 in 2027; gasoline at $3.91 and $3.56.
body: The October Short-Term Energy Outlook, released Oct. 6, reads at first like a relief story. EIA expects Brent to average $105 per barrel in the fourth quarter, below the $114 average it recorded for September, and to fall to an $84 annual average in 2027. Its WTI path runs from about $97 in 4Q26 to $79.74 next year.

The detail behind that path is less comfortable. EIA's forecast rests on supply returning, not on demand weakening, and it assumes oil flows from the Middle East remain constrained through the fourth quarter.

EIA puts Middle East shut-in production at 4.8 million barrels a day in September, less than half the 10.9 million b/d peak in May. But it forecasts 4.5 million b/d of shut-ins for 4Q26, barely better than September. The agency also notes that attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline temporarily halted a key bypass route around the Strait of Hormuz, and that tanker rates hit record levels in September, adding to delivered crude costs.

The more important number may be the stock draw. EIA estimates global oil inventories fell by an average of 1.9 million b/d in the third quarter and expects a further draw of about 0.7 million b/d in the fourth. A smaller draw is still a draw: the market is entering winter with less buffer than it had in the summer, and EIA says prices will stay elevated until constraints on Middle East oil flows resolve, then ease gradually as depleted inventories rebuild next year.

Diesel is where that shows up first. East Coast distillate inventories were 32% below their five-year seasonal average in September, and EIA expects them to stay about 20% below average through the winter. It forecasts retail diesel at $5.19 a gallon for 2026. That fits the Dallas Fed's Beige Book report that diesel is the top cost driver in its district.

For markets, the outlook explains why September's energy-led inflation jump is unlikely to fade quickly. Diesel feeds freight, farming and goods costs with a lag, so even if crude eases as EIA expects, the pass-through from distillates can keep pressure on goods prices into early 2027. Natural gas is the exception: EIA sees Henry Hub averaging $3.48 per MMBtu this year and $3.16 in 2027, with above-average storage heading into the heating season.

The next official check comes Thursday, when EIA publishes its weekly petroleum data, delayed a day by Monday's federal closure. The distillate line will show whether winter supply is rebuilding or whether EIA's below-average assumption is, if anything, optimistic.

items.title: The Close: Bank earnings show growth, with credit and compliance bills attached
items.dek: Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, State Street and BlackRock all grew revenue in the third quarter, while the Fed's H.15 shows long Treasury yields easing off last week's levels.
key_points: Citigroup earned $2.85 a diluted share on $23.8 billion of revenue, with net interest income up 14% and a $2.6 billion provision for credit losses.
Bank of America's revenue rose to $29.96 billion from $29.04 billion, but net income fell to $6.93 billion after a $1.2 billion Bank Secrecy Act-related charge.
Wells Fargo's diluted EPS rose to $1.87 from $1.66 on revenue of $21.87 billion.
State Street revenue rose about 13% to $4.0 billion and BlackRock revenue rose about 19% to $7.75 billion.
Per the Fed's H.15, the 10-year Treasury yield was 5.21% on October 13, down from 5.28% on October 7; the 2-year was 4.79%.
body: The heart of the third-quarter bank reporting season has now arrived, and the message from the official filings is consistent: revenue is growing almost everywhere, but the path from revenue to earnings runs through credit costs, regulatory bills and capital return decisions that differ sharply by firm.

body.h: Citi's operating leverage, with a card-loss price tag

body: Citigroup reported net income of $5.2 billion, or $2.85 per diluted share, versus $3.8 billion, or $1.86, a year earlier. Revenues rose to $23.8 billion from $22.1 billion, net interest income rose 14% and reported operating expenses fell 2% to $14.0 billion. The year-ago quarter carried a Banamex-related goodwill impairment, so the EPS jump overstates the underlying change, but revenue growing faster than expenses is real. The cost is in credit: the provision was $2.6 billion, including $2.2 billion of net credit losses and a $369 million net reserve build. Citi still returned $4.1 billion to shareholders with its CET1 ratio at 12.8%.

body.h: Wells Fargo and Bank of America

body: Wells Fargo earned $5.95 billion, or $1.87 per diluted share, up from $1.66, on total revenue of $21.87 billion against $21.44 billion. EPS grew far faster than revenue, a reminder that share count and cost discipline are doing much of the work. Bank of America went the other way on the bottom line: revenue rose to $29.96 billion from $29.04 billion, but net income fell to $6.93 billion from $8.33 billion, and diluted EPS to $0.91 from $1.04, after a $1.2 billion charge for Bank Secrecy Act-related civil money penalties.

body.h: Fee businesses and the industrial read

body: State Street's revenue rose to $4.00 billion from $3.55 billion and diluted EPS to $3.69 from $2.78. BlackRock's revenue rose to $7.75 billion from $6.51 billion, with GAAP diluted EPS of $10.57 versus $8.43. Outside finance, Fastenal's net sales rose to $2.46 billion from $2.13 billion, a constructive signal for U.S. industrial demand.

The Fed's H.15 release shows the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.21% on October 13, down from 5.28% on October 7, and the 30-year at 5.56% from 5.67%. The 2-year held at 4.79% and the 3-month constant-maturity yield edged up to 4.26%, well above the 3.88% effective federal funds rate. The long end has eased while the front end has not, which keeps pressure on bank funding costs even as longer-dated borrowing rates get some relief.

AlphaGen's read: the large banks are entering the final quarter of 2026 with growing revenue and solid capital, so the swing factors for earnings are now credit losses and one-off charges, not demand for financial services. The FOMC meets October 27–28.

items.title: Q3 financials: fee engines are carrying the quarter
items.dek: BlackRock and State Street posted double-digit revenue growth on market-linked fees, while Bank of America and Wells Fargo show balance-sheet banks paying for compliance and building reserves.
key_points: BlackRock's AUM rose 15% to $15.5 trillion on $205 billion of Q3 net inflows; revenue rose 19% to $7.75 billion.
State Street's total revenue rose 13% to $4.0 billion, with fee revenue up 11% and net interest income up 21%; AUC/A reached a record $59.2 trillion.
Bank of America's Q3 net income fell to $6.9 billion from $8.3 billion, including a $1.2 billion charge for Bank Secrecy Act-related civil money penalties; net interest income rose 8%.
Wells Fargo's provision for credit losses rose to $1.03 billion from $681 million, partly on higher allowances for commercial and industrial and auto loans.
body: The first wave of third-quarter results from U.S. financials splits cleanly in two. Firms paid on the value of assets they manage or hold are growing revenue at double-digit rates. Balance-sheet banks are growing more slowly and are absorbing costs that have nothing to do with the cycle.

BlackRock ended the quarter with $15.5 trillion in assets under management, up 15% from a year earlier, after $205 billion of net inflows. Revenue rose 19% to $7.75 billion and as-adjusted diluted EPS rose 38% to $15.93. The company put annualized organic base fee growth at 11% for the quarter, which is the cleanest measure of growth that markets did not simply hand over.

State Street tells a similar story from the custody side. Total revenue rose 13% to $4.0 billion, fee revenue rose 11%, and net interest income rose 21%. Assets under custody and/or administration reached a record $59.2 trillion. Fee revenue is still roughly 78% of the total, so the business remains tied to asset levels and client activity more than to rates.

Bank of America reported net income of $6.9 billion, or $0.91 a share, down from $8.3 billion, or $1.04. The quarter carried a $1.2 billion non-tax-deductible charge, or $0.17 a share, to accrue for civil money penalties tied to consent orders on its Bank Secrecy Act program. Strip that out and the operating picture is steady: revenue rose 3%, net interest income rose 8%, and the provision for credit losses was roughly flat at $1.3 billion.

Wells Fargo, which reported on October 13, earned $1.87 a share versus $1.66 a year earlier. Its provision for credit losses rose to $1.03 billion from $681 million, partly on higher allowances for commercial and industrial and auto loans, and its estimated CET1 ratio was 10.0%, down from 11.0% a year earlier, after $2.5 billion of buybacks in the quarter.

Our read is that Q3 rewards scale in fee businesses and exposes the costs of running large balance sheets. In this set of releases, market-linked revenue is doing more of the work than lending spreads. For credit investors, nothing in these releases points to stress in the large-bank complex. Wells Fargo's reserve build and lower CET1 ratio are the details worth tracking into year-end, because they show where management sees risk and how much buffer it is willing to give up for buybacks.

items.title: September CPI: an energy shock, not a broad reacceleration
items.dek: Headline inflation jumped to 3.7% on gasoline, while core held at 2.6%. The gap between the two is now the central question for the Fed on October 28.
key_points: Headline CPI rose 0.6% in September after 0.4% in August; the 12-month rate is 3.7%.
Gasoline rose 9.1% on the month and accounted for over half of the headline increase.
Core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% on the year. Energy is up 20.4% year over year.
The FOMC meets October 27–28, with the decision on the 28th.
body: September's CPI report delivered a hot headline and a calm core. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the all-items index rose 0.6% on a seasonally adjusted basis, after a 0.4% gain in August, lifting the 12-month rate to 3.7%.

The driver was energy. Gasoline rose 9.1% in September and accounted for over half of the monthly increase. The energy index is now up 20.4% from a year earlier. Strip out food and energy and the picture changes: core CPI rose 0.3% on the month and 2.6% over the past year.

A 110-basis-point spread between headline and core inflation tells you this is a supply shock moving through one category, not demand running hot across the economy. That distinction drives policy. A central bank can look through an energy spike if it stays contained. It cannot ignore it if fuel costs start showing up in transportation, goods, and services prices.
Shelter is the piece to watch for that spillover. It rose 0.4% on the month and 3.2% on the year, and as the stickiest major category it is where broad pressure would show up first.

The bond market's job between now and October 28 is to price how the Fed reads this report. With the 10-year Treasury yield already above 5%, a hotter headline narrows the room for error in long-duration assets. For equities, the read-through is about margins: an energy shock acts like a tax on consumers and an input-cost squeeze on companies outside the energy sector.

Our view: the core number is the one the Fed is most likely to anchor on, but headline inflation at 3.7% raises the cost of sounding relaxed. The tell on October 28 is whether the statement addresses energy pass-through directly.
